chapters.title: Chapter 3: Momentum Indicators - RSI, ROC, and Combining Signals

lessons.title: Rate of Change (ROC): The Simplest Momentum Measure

children.text: Everything built in Chapter 2 measured trend indirectly, through the relationship between two smoothed averages of price. This chapter switches to a different family of tools, momentum indicators that measure a stock's speed of movement directly, without needing a second moving average to compare against. The simplest of these, and the one closest to how Chapter 1 originally defined momentum, is the rate of change, ROC.

body.text: Rate of change measures exactly how much a security's price has moved over a fixed look-back window, expressed as a percentage. It is the most literal possible implementation of the momentum idea from Chapter 1: how much has this price changed over the last n periods?

body.caption: The n-period rate of change: today's price compared to the price n periods ago, expressed as a percentage.

children.text: A positive ROC means the price is higher than it was n periods ago, positive momentum. A negative ROC means the opposite. Unlike a moving average, ROC uses only two data points, today's price and the price from n periods back, it does not average anything in between.
Worked Example: The Same Ten Days From Chapter 2

Reuse the ten illustrative closing prices from Chapter 2, Lesson 1: 100, 102, 101, 104, 106, 105, 108, 110, 109, 112. A 5-day ROC needs at least 5 days of prior data, so the first value is available on Day 6.

body.caption: 5-day ROC on the same illustrative closing prices used in Chapter 2 (rounded to 2 decimals)

body.text: Notice how much more this bounces around than the smooth SMA and EMA lines from Chapter 2 did on the exact same prices. ROC has no smoothing built in at all, it is comparing two single points, which makes it faster to reflect a new move but also noisier day to day.

markDefs.definition: A technical indicator that fluctuates around a fixed centre value, typically zero, with crossings of that centre used as directional signals.

children.text: Because ROC is expressed as a percentage change, it naturally oscillates around zero rather than tracking price on its own scale, which is why it belongs to a family of tools called

. A trader can build a signal purely from ROC crossing above or below zero, buy when ROC turns positive, sell or short when it turns negative, without needing any second moving average at all. This is a fundamentally different construction from the crossover systems in Chapter 2, even though both are ultimately trying to answer the same question about trend direction.

A short window, 5 to 10 trading days, makes ROC fast and reactive, useful for spotting a sharp near-term acceleration but prone to whipsaws in choppy conditions, much like a fast EMA. A long window, 126 trading days for roughly 6 months or 252 for roughly a year, turns ROC into essentially the same measurement used to define momentum academically in Chapter 1: the trailing return over a formation period. This is not a coincidence. A 126-day ROC on a stock is, in substance, the same calculation as the 6-month trailing return used to rank stocks in a cross-sectional momentum system, including the Nifty200 Momentum 30 Index covered in Chapter 1. Short-window ROC and long-window ROC are the same formula answering two different questions, one about near-term speed, one about medium-term trend strength.

columns.label: Rate of Change (ROC)
points: Compares today's price to the price n periods ago directly
No smoothing, reacts immediately to the latest price
A long-window ROC is essentially a trailing-return momentum score

columns.label: Moving Average Crossover
points: Compares two smoothed averages of price to each other
Smoothed twice over, reacts more slowly by construction
No natural zero line, just a relative comparison
Built to define trend regime, not raw speed

body.caption: Computing 5-day ROC in pandas
body.code:
import pandas as pd

close = pd.Series([100, 102, 101, 104, 106, 105, 108, 110, 109, 112])

roc_5 = close.pct_change(periods=5) * 100
print(roc_5.round(2))

body.text: A raw ROC crossing zero is exactly as prone to whipsaws in a genuinely sideways market as the raw crossover system from Chapter 2 was. ROC is rarely traded completely on its own for this reason, it is usually smoothed, combined with a trend filter, or blended with another signal, the subject of the next lesson.

body.title: Calculate a 10-day ROC
body.prompt: A stock closes at ₹250 today. Ten trading days ago it closed at ₹200. What is its 10-day ROC, in percent?
body.explanation: (250 - 200) / 200 x 100 = 50 / 200 x 100 = 25%. The stock is 25% higher than it was 10 trading days ago.

body.title: What makes ROC different from a moving average?
body.question: Which statement correctly describes a key difference between ROC and a moving average?
options: ROC can only be calculated on indices, not individual stocks
ROC compares two single price points directly, while a moving average smooths many prices together, making ROC noisier but faster to react
A moving average is always more accurate than ROC in every market condition
ROC and a moving average are mathematically identical formulas
body.explanation: ROC uses only two data points, today's price and the price n periods back, with no averaging in between. A moving average smooths many prices together. That difference is exactly why ROC reacts faster but bounces around more.

body.description: TradingView includes Rate of Change as a built-in indicator that can be overlaid below any NSE or BSE stock's price chart, useful for building visual intuition for how it moves relative to price.

cards.definition: The percentage change in a security's price over a fixed look-back window of n periods, comparing only today's price to the price n periods ago.
A technical indicator that fluctuates around a fixed centre value, typically zero, with crossings of that centre used as directional signals.
The number of periods back ROC compares today's price against, ranging from a few days for a fast, reactive signal to several months for a momentum-style trailing return.

points: ROC measures the percentage change in price over a fixed look-back window, comparing only two data points, today's price and the price n periods ago.
It oscillates around a zero line, letting it generate signals on its own, without needing a second moving average for comparison.

A short ROC window is fast and noisy, closer to an EMA in behaviour. A long ROC window, 126 or 252 trading days, is essentially the same calculation as the trailing-return momentum score used in Chapter 1's cross-sectional momentum ranking.
ROC reacts faster than a moving average because it has no smoothing built in, but this also makes it more prone to whipsaws on its own.
ROC is rarely traded in isolation. Smoothing it or combining it with another signal, covered in the next lesson, is standard practice.
